See out/recon/tasks/T020/CLASS/d723b7b66951bef8/attempt*.log for the full trace.
capabilities.additional_confirmation_2026-11-22: 5 more attempts this same day, all killed at the identical step (loading datapack.unity3d, before any object is read), confirmed via journalctl -k each time. Resident memory at the moment of the kill varied widely across attempts - 3.66GB, 3.75GB, and 5.78GB RSS in three different runs - which rules out a fixed per-process ceiling; it is global host memory pressure at the moment of the call (observed culprit: a user's Chrome instance with many renderer processes, sometimes 2GB+ alone) that decides whether this specific load survives, not a property of the Python process itself. 'RAM available' read from `free -m` right before launching the load did NOT reliably predict the outcome (one attempt was launched with 2.6GB available/1.6GB swap free and still died; see LOOP_STATE.md 2026-11-21/22 entries for the full timeline across all attempts).

evidence: open_binary succeeded fast for both 'hopper' and 'ghidra' provider_id (hash of libil2cpp.so confirmed: b63661fa60c2...), and binary_session reported both providers' availability.status as 'available' beforehand.

Hopper: any analysis call (analyze_function) hung and returned provider_timeout after 120s, with launcher stderr showing 'QObject::disconnect: wildcard call disconnects from destroyed signal of QDialog::WaitDialog' - Hopper is stuck on a modal dialog (license/loader) with no GUI available in this headless sandbox to dismiss it. Same symptom already noted in LOOP_STATE.md from an earlier session (T034 _st investigation).

Ghidra: analyze_function on one address timed out at 330000ms; a SECOND, much lighter call (inspect_native_instruction, a single-address decode) ALSO ran past 120s before being stopped. This shows every call triggers Ghidra's full AnalyzeHeadless import+auto-analysis pipeline from a fresh temp project each time (-deleteProject, no cache between MCP calls) rather than a per-function lazy analysis - so there is no 'ask for just one small thing' escape hatch via this bridge. The JVM process itself is memory-bounded (-Xmx2G heap cap observed in `ps`), so this did NOT produce an OOM kill this time (unlike UnityPy/datapack below) - it is a wall-clock timeout, with host swap dropping as low as 132MB free during the run.
limits: Neither Hopper nor Ghidra is currently usable through this REA bridge in this sandboxed environment for even a single targeted lookup - Hopper needs interactive GUI dismissal of a stuck dialog; Ghidra's bridge always redoes a full-binary headless analysis pass (multiple minutes) per call, with no persistence across calls.

Lighter REA read tools that do NOT require a provider's deep-analysis run (binary_session, open_binary itself) work fine and are cheap - the wall only appears once an analysis-dependent tool (analyze_function, inspect_native_instruction, procedure_pseudo_code, resolve_native_call_targets, etc.) is called.

known_limits_summary: The single hard blocker reconfirmed across two sessions (2026-11-21, 2026-11-22) is host memory: loading datapack.unity3d (>1GB) via UnityPy reliably OOMs on this 7.3GB-RAM/4GB-swap host at a varying RSS threshold (3.66-5.78GB observed), regardless of thread count or the RAM 'available' reading at launch time - this is global host memory pressure, not a fixed per-process ceiling.

Everything that stays within libil2cpp.so + global-metadata.dat + small cached JSON/jsonl/gz indexes (ARM64 method contracts, scene-root lookups, class/field name joins, and now full type-tree generation for triage) works reliably and was used successfully across both sessions.
Unity Editor batch builds work but contend heavily for the same scarce RAM; running one alongside UnityPy-on-datapack or another Editor instance is not reliable on this host.

REA's Hopper and Ghidra deep-analysis providers are both currently unusable in this sandbox for any analysis-dependent call (not just heavy ones) - Hopper hangs on a stuck GUI dialog, Ghidra always redoes a full-binary headless analysis pass per call with no cross-call cache, hitting a wall-clock timeout before an OOM would even be reached.
